extracted.intended_audience: princes, rulers, political leaders, and students of statecraft
extracted.subtask_description: Practical maxims for acquiring and retaining political power in a principality: how a prince should manage subjects, soldiers, reputation, cruelty, faith, fortifications, and conspiracies. Emphasises prudence, appearance, and the pragmatic use of force and deceit where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer being feared to being loved (but avoid hatred)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is much safer to be feared than loved, when, of the two, either must be dispensed with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because men are ungrateful and fickle, fear preserves a prince by a dread of punishment which never fails. Nevertheless a prince ought to inspire fear in such a way that, if he does not win love, he avoids hatred; he can endure being feared whilst he is not hated, which will be as long as he abstains from the property of his citizens and subjects and from their women.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid seizing subjects' property or violating their women
rubrics_metrics.description: A prince must abstain from the property of his citizens and subjects and from their women.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Men more quickly forget the death of their father than the loss of their patrimony; pretexts for taking property are never wanting and will breed lasting hatred. Thus a prince should avoid actions that touch property or honor to prevent hatred.

rubrics_metrics.name: If killing is necessary, do so with justification and manifest cause
rubrics_metrics.description: When it is necessary for him to proceed against the life of someone, he must do it on proper justification and for manifest cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Taking life is harder for people to forgive than taking property; therefore executions or killings should be clearly justified to limit resentment and avoid hatred when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: When commanding soldiers, be willing to appear cruel
rubrics_metrics.description: When a prince is with his army and has under control a multitude of soldiers, it is quite necessary for him to disregard the reputation of cruelty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without a reputation for cruelty he would never hold his army united or disposed to its duties (example: Hannibal’s inhuman cruelty kept diverse troops together). Military discipline may require harsher measures that would be unwise in civil contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use both force and cunning: be a lion and a fox
rubrics_metrics.description: A prince ought to be a fox to discover snares and a lion to terrify wolves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There are two ways of contesting — by law (proper to men) and by force (proper to beasts). A prince must know how to use both natures; relying solely on the lion or solely on the fox is insufficient. Historical examples (Achilles, many princes) teach this balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep faith when possible, but know when to break it
rubrics_metrics.description: A wise lord cannot, nor ought he to, keep faith when such observance may be turned against him, and when the reasons that caused him to pledge it exist no longer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although keeping faith is praiseworthy, princes who have done great things have held good faith of little account and used craft. If others will not be faithful, a prince is not bound to observe faith with them; legitimate reasons will always be found to excuse non-observance (example: Alexander VI deceived successfully).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appear virtuous even if you are not
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unnecessary for a prince to have all the good qualities, but it is very necessary to appear to have them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To appear merciful, faithful, humane, religious, upright is useful; to actually have and always observe them may be injurious. A prince should cultivate the appearance of these qualities because men judge largely by what they see.

rubrics_metrics.name: Control public image because most judge by appearances
rubrics_metrics.description: Men judge generally more by the eye than by the hand, because it belongs to everybody to see you, to few to come in touch with you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that what is seen and heard about the prince makes him appear merciful, faithful, humane, upright, and religious; few know the truth and those few dare not oppose the opinion of the many backed by state majesty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid being considered contemptible (fickle, effeminate, irresolute)
rubrics_metrics.description: A prince should guard against being considered fickle, frivolous, effeminate, mean‑spirited, irresolute; he should show greatness, courage, gravity, and fortitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A contemptible reputation invites plots and makes maintaining authority difficult. In private dealings, let judgments be irrevocable and maintain a reputation that prevents deception or subversion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent hatred and secure popular goodwill to deter conspiracies
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the most efficacious remedies against conspiracies is not to be hated and despised by the people; keep the people satisfied with him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A conspirator expects popular support; if removal of the prince will not please the people, conspirators lose incentive. Examples: Bentivogli’s murder followed by popular vengeance; well‑ordered states keep nobles from desperation and keep people content to avoid plots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage nobles and people carefully; delegate unpopular acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Princes ought to cherish the nobles, but not so as to make themselves hated by the people; leave affairs of reproach to the management of others, and keep those of grace in their own hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set up impartial arbiters (example: French parliament) to check nobles and protect people, thereby avoiding direct blame to the prince. Keep honors and gracious acts in the prince’s control while unpopular measures can be carried out by intermediaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise which group to appease (people vs soldiers) depending on state type
rubrics_metrics.description: Except for the Turk and the Soldan, it is now more necessary to all princes to satisfy the people rather than the soldiers; in states governed by soldiers, keep the soldiers' favour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical Roman emperors failed or succeeded depending on how they balanced soldiers and people; new princes must judge whether to placate the army or the populace according to local military/political structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arm or disarm subjects strategically
rubrics_metrics.description: A new prince in a new principality has always distributed arms; when adding a new province to an old state it is necessary to disarm the men of that state except those who were his adherents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arming loyal supporters makes them dependents and creates a core of adherents; disarming conquered provinces reduces the risk of rebellion. Avoid total disarmament that signals distrust and breeds hatred; otherwise one must rely on mercenaries (unreliable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid fostering local factions as a durable policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Fostering quarrels or factions among subject towns may be useful in some times but is not a general precept; factions are risky and can fail when an enemy attacks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fostering divisions may prevent unity against the prince in peace, but in wartime a divided city quickly falls as the weaker party aids the enemy. Such methods indicate weakness and are only useful under narrow conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build fortresses only after weighing tradeoffs
rubrics_metrics.description: Fortresses are useful or not according to circumstances; they can serve as a bridle to those who might work against the prince and as a refuge from a first attack, but they can also injure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: some princes demolished fortresses to make states easier to keep; others praised fortresses. Decide based on particulars of the state — fortresses may help in defense but can also become liabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer recruits who had been distrusted because they have incentive to prove loyalty
rubrics_metrics.description: Those men who at the commencement of a principality have been hostile but were gained over can be held tightly and serve the prince with fidelity; they often yield more than those who served securely under the old government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If men favoured you only from discontent with their prior government they will be harder to keep; weigh motivations before rewarding early supporters. Generally, men who have been distrusted initially and then benefited have more reason to prove themselves.
